hero.headline: Beetlejuice Musical Runs Through June 7 at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit runs through Saturday at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, bringing spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
Beetlejuice the musical is playing at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach through June 7. Running June 2 through June 7, the Broadway hit brings its spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments to the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen, whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. I get to break the fourth wall a lot, so I get to communicate directly to the audience and share some moments with them, he explained. Very early in the run, he experienced one of those unexpected moments. I have a wig change on stage that Im wearing two wigs. The second wig came off with the first wig, so I was bald for an entire scene, and I got to play with that a little bit, and got to experience everyone seeing me for the first time and not knowing that I am bald.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50, and the safest and most secure way to get them is to buy directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: Florida Senate Sends Homestead Property Tax Cut to November Ballot
cards.body:
Floridians will vote in November on whether to dramatically reduce homestead property taxes after the Senate voted 30-9 to place HJR 1-F on the ballot. The House passed the measure 75-26. The constitutional amendment is a major priority of Governor Ron DeSantis.

If approved by at least 60% of voters, the amendment would increase homestead exemptions for primary residences to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for those who own homes in the state by the end of this year. Further increases would be tied to the Consumer Price Index. School taxes would not be subject to the increased exemption limit and would remain at $25,000.

The measure could put money in homeowners' pockets across the state. County and city officials have warned the effort could wreak havoc on local budgets as reduced property tax revenue affects municipal services and infrastructure funding.

Floridians who own primary residences as of the end of 2026 would be eligible for the expanded exemption beginning in 2027. The vote will take place on the November ballot, requiring support from at least 60% of voters to amend the state constitution. The measure represents one of the most significant property tax reduction proposals to reach Florida voters in recent years.

cards.headline: President Trump Nominates Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez as Ambassador to Brazil
cards.teaser: House Speaker Daniel Perez, who spent two years leading the Florida House and publicly battling Governor DeSantis, has been nominated by President Donald Trump to serve as U.S. Ambassador to Brazil.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump has nominated Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez as U.S. Ambassador to Brazil, the largest country in South America and one of the United States' most significant trade and diplomatic partners in the region. The nomination was part of a broader batch of appointments Trump sent to the Senate, which also included four other Florida nominees for ambassador and federal law enforcement posts.

Perez spent the past two years leading the Florida House, publicly battling DeSantis while moving the Legislature toward a more coequal footing. The nomination comes just under nine months after the White House urged Perez to run for Florida Attorney General, an undertaking he declined to pursue that would have put him on a collision course with DeSantis appointee James Uthmeier.

cards.headline: Ocean could breach Jupiter Island at Peck Lake, potentially splitting island in half
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island faces severe coastal erosion across its entire 11.5-mile shoreline. The most concerning threat is at Peck Lake, where a breach could split the island in half by turning a thin strip of land into an open inlet. This risk extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand, demonstrating that such events are not merely theoretical concerns.

The erosion threatens far more than just the physical coastline. Roads, buildings, and drainage systems face damage, but the report also documents risks to natural habitats, wildlife, and archaeological sites. Among the most significant is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old site that has already lost half its area to erosion. Other endangered locations include Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society noted that more than 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. Perry explained that future breaches could destabilize ecosystems dependent on a careful balance between fresh and saltwater environments. He emphasized the urgency of the situation, stating "the last 15 years, it's been rising at a faster rate" regarding sea level rise since the 1950s.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town actively combats erosion through ongoing maintenance efforts. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project that deposited enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field stressed that oceanfront homes remain safe only because of these continuous interventions. He described the approach as "just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," acknowledging it is a temporary solution. The town invests approximately $3 million in annual taxpayer funding toward beach renourishment.

However, this funding strategy depends on continued financial support. If a breach occurs, Field warned that repairs would require substantial state and federal investment. He cautioned that "if funding ever goes away for beach renourishment in Florida, the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly, and not in a way that anybody's particularly happy with." Field noted that the recent FDEP assessment should help Jupiter Island compete more effectively for state and federal funding to address erosion. The report positions the island to make a stronger case for future financial support to mitigate these mounting coastal threats.

cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are investigating allegations of child abuse, starvation and filthy conditions inside a pastor's home.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police are investigating allegations of child abuse, starvation and filthy conditions inside a pastor's home. Officers discovered the alleged abuse during an investigation at the residence.

Police found evidence of possible child neglect and poor living conditions at the home. The pastor now faces serious allegations related to the welfare of children in the home.

The investigation continues as authorities work to determine the full extent of the alleged abuse and neglect. Child welfare officials are involved in the case.

cards.headline: Florida May Ban Fourth of July Fireworks Due to Severe Drought Conditions
cards.teaser: State leaders are watching drought conditions closely as they weigh whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence, with drought conditions more severe than 1998.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services is monitoring severe drought conditions as state leaders consider banning fireworks for Fourth of July celebrations. The current drought is more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was implemented. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about a potential ban in May. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said. He acknowledged the significance of the 250th anniversary celebration but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, owner Bill Murphy reported increased customer activity ahead of the holiday as people shop early. Murphy said the store monitors drought conditions closely but remains cautiously optimistic, noting that rain is forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

hero.headline: Fertilizer Ban Takes Effect June 1 in Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River Counties
hero.body:
Starting June 1, residents across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop applying fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen to their lawns and landscaping. The restriction runs through the rainy season and aims to prevent nutrient-laden runoff from flowing into local waterways, where it can trigger algae blooms that harm aquatic ecosystems.

The seasonal ban targets a significant environmental problem in the region. Jordan Skaggs, who works with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that the measure protects waterways including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. When algae blooms form in these bodies of water, they can block sunlight from reaching beneficial aquatic plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. In severe cases, harmful algae blooms produce toxins with serious consequences. According to Skaggs, "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health."

Residents looking for alternatives during the ban should consider composting, according to Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension. Composting provides an effective way to add necessary nutrients back into garden soil and landscaping without relying on commercial fertilizers. Ricketts described the approach as simple and accessible. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape."

The prohibition covers all fertilizer applications containing the restricted nutrients, regardless of where residents plan to use them on their properties. Those who fail to comply with the seasonal restriction face potential penalties enforced by local code enforcement officials. Property owners should review their landscaping maintenance plans now to ensure they have alternatives in place before the June 1 deadline.

cards.headline: Florida Voters Divided on Property Tax Homestead Exemption Proposal
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, a proposal drawing mixed reactions in West Palm Beach.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes for homeowners. The ballot measure would need 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018.

Brian Edington supports the proposal because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida. "I think it's a really good idea because it saves the people that really live in Florida, the homeowners," Edington said. He said he is comfortable with local governments having to spend less and pointed to his own neighborhood trash services as an example. "I have trash services in my neighborhood, they pick it up twice, I don't need it twice a week, once a week would be adequate," Edington said. While homeowners were generally supportive of paying less in taxes, renters expressed more skepticism. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach them. "Pretty sure they're going to raise the rent on everybody, all the renters, I'm pretty sure they're going to raise those taxes," the renter said.

cards.headline: Florida Supreme Court Adopts New AI Rules for Courtrooms After Rampant Misuse
cards.teaser: Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants will soon be required to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate under new rules taking effect June 15.
cards.body:
The Florida Supreme Court recently adopted new rules addressing the misuse of artificial intelligence in courtrooms, a crisis that has prompted the state's highest court to act. The rules take effect June 15 and will require Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate. Fake evidence, fabricated facts and bogus case law have become widespread concerns in Florida courtrooms. Sanctions for violations could range from a public reprimand to fines and even suspension.

Federal Judge William Matthewman, chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, has been involved in efforts to control how AI is used in courts after witnessing its misuse firsthand. "It's really a problem," Matthewman said, adding, "Unfortunately, I see it getting worse before it gets better." In Polk County, an attorney representing the Polk County School District in a lawsuit over school bus cameras was chastised after a judge discovered fabricated facts and cases that don't exist in a motion to dismiss. The attorney admitted to using ChatGPT as a drafting and research aid but said there was no excuse for failing to verify the information before filing. Matthewman cautioned anyone filing court documents to ensure accuracy. "If not, you could find yourself in hot water," he said.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County Woman Sues Campbell Soup, Walmart Over Alleged Worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: A woman from Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter found live worms in their SpaghettiOs after eating them and developed parasitic infections and other medical complications.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart, seeking $50,000 in damages after she and her daughter allegedly found live worms in SpaghettiOs they purchased in June 2024. The product was bought at the Walmart Supercenter store on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the lawsuit, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. She documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the product.

Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications from consuming the contaminated food. The lawsuit alleges that Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart failed to properly inspect the product before it reached consumers. Campbell Soup Co. responded by saying the claims lack merit, while Walmart stated it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Florida Dive Operators Fight Federal Shark Feeding Ban
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry, with operators warning it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses.
cards.body:
The Safe Florida Seas Act, known as H.R. 3831, would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters have called it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, a coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said no one from Congress has yet asked dive operators to present data or explain their practices. Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives. They argue this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface.

Florida operators point to Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as a cautionary tale. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased, fatalities have been reported and, according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. In a letter sent to Congress, Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

This case highlights ongoing concerns about food safety and quality control in mass-produced products. The incident, alleged to have occurred in June 2024, adds to a growing list of product liability cases involving food contamination. Both companies face pressure to address the allegations and demonstrate their commitment to consumer safety through their quality assurance processes.

He emphasized that composting is both practical and accessible for most homeowners.

The fertilizer restrictions represent a proactive measure taken by these three counties to protect their natural resources during the season when heavy rainfall increases the risk of nutrient runoff reaching local waterways. By reducing the application of nitrogen and phosphorus-based products, officials hope to minimize conditions that trigger destructive algae blooms while encouraging residents to adopt more sustainable landscaping practices.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties could lose hundreds of millions under property tax plan
cards.teaser: Local governments are working to assess the impact of a property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and cut property tax bills, with potential losses in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
cards.body:
Government officials are assessing the impact of a property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said officials are working with administrators and the Office of Management and Budget to determine the potential effects. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated significant losses for Treasure Coast counties: Martin County would lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29, St. Lucie County would lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29, and Indian River County would lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29.

Powell said if property taxes are cut, there will be real shortfalls and challenges requiring revenue to be made up elsewhere. The referendum, which would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal benefits struggling families in homes valued around $300,000. Local officials are restricted by the state from speaking against or endorsing the referendum but can provide educational information.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition begins for mixed-use redevelopment in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: Crews began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project at the Vero Beach shopping center.
cards.body:
Crews began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall this week for a revitalization project at the shopping center. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager for the redevelopment, said the first phase involves taking down the Macy's and the former Sears location. Neighbors watched the demolition from the mall parking lot. Mary Alice Stopyra said she is happy the mall is being torn down because it has degraded over time. Mark Manera from Vero Beach said the mall looked like a graveyard and described seeing a steady decline year after year. Manera added that if the redevelopment brings new life, new jobs and new opportunity, "that's wonderful."

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He described the vision as "a city within a city" instead of the dead mall that has been getting cobwebs for the last 12 years. Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027. The project team is still working on permitting for the rest of the development.

Ron DeSantis, argue that local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending excessively.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell warned that the property tax cuts will create significant challenges. A study from the Florida Association of Counties estimates Palm Beach County could lose $280 million in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29. Powell said local officials are exploring options including finding new revenue and implementing budget cuts, though the specific mechanisms remain uncertain. "We don't know if it will be an increase in sales tax, we don't know if it will be an increase in user fees for other services," Powell said. Homeowner savings will vary from hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on county, city and assessed home value. Over half of Palm Beach County properties currently have the homestead exemption.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program overwhelmed by demand
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County receives nearly 8,000 calls per month for housing assistance, but the Emergency Rental Assistance Program has limited funding and fills up within hours each month.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, designed to help residents who cannot pay rent. Program director Dr. James Green told WPTV that every month the demand far outweighs available funds. The county receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month based on combined data with 211, and currently has about 800 applications in the queue for rental assistance.

Applications open at the beginning of each month but fill quickly, with the county typically receiving about 600 applications in the first couple of hours they are open. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Green said the recent surge in applications is partly due to rising costs of living including housing, gas, and food. For those who cannot access the county's program, 211 is another option where teams will connect callers with nonprofits and other assistance programs in the area.

hero.headline: Florida voters weigh property tax cuts ahead of November vote
hero.teaser: Florida voters will decide in November whether to raise the homestead exemption for homeowners, drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure would need 60% approval to pass.
hero.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to approve a ballot measure that would reduce property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners. The proposal has sparked varying opinions among West Palm Beach residents as the election approaches. To become law, the measure needs at least 60% voter approval. Notably, a similar proposal failed to pass in 2018.

Local officials are still calculating how much revenue cities and counties would lose if the measure passes, and the specific areas where budget cuts might occur remain uncertain. Brian Edington supports the proposal because he believes it benefits people who permanently live in Florida as homeowners. He expressed comfort with the idea of local governments operating with reduced budgets. As an example, he pointed to trash collection in his neighborhood, suggesting that weekly pickup would be sufficient instead of the current twice-weekly service.

However, some residents worry about the consequences of reduced government funding. Rosabella Olivares raised concerns about what lower funding could mean for essential services, noting that expenses are already high. Another resident named Stan said he does not want funding eliminated entirely, though he acknowledged that some reduction could help people. One Florida resident advocated for a different approach, suggesting that the tax system should be tied more directly to the specific services people actually use, such as schools.

While homeowners generally showed support for paying less in taxes, renters expressed greater skepticism about the proposal's benefits. A renter interviewed along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the tax savings would not reach renters directly. This resident predicted that landlords would respond to the tax cuts by raising rents on tenants to offset any losses, meaning renters would not experience the financial relief that homeowners would gain from the measure. This concern highlights a key divide in how different groups view the potential impact of the property tax reduction proposal.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County faces $140 million loss from property tax proposal
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29 if voters approve a property tax referendum in November. County officials are working to determine the impact of the new homestead exemption proposal.
cards.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of a property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. According to a study from the Florida Association of Counties, St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Other counties face significant losses as well: Martin County is estimated to lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29, Indian River County could lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29, and Palm Beach County faces potential losses of $280 million in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29.

The referendum will raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with voters deciding in November. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said that if property taxes are cut, there will be real shortfalls and revenue will have to be made up somewhere, possibly through increases in sales tax or user fees. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal provides a break for struggling families in homes valued around $300,000. The savings for homeowners can vary from hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on county, city, and assessed home value.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach for mixed-use redevelopment
cards.teaser: Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project for the shopping center.
cards.body:
Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project for the shopping center. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager working on the redevelopment, said crews are working on the first phase: taking down the Macy's and soon the former Sears location. Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra said she was happy to see the mall torn down because it had degraded over time. Mark Manera, who has been coming to the mall for years, described it as looking like a graveyard with a steady decline year after year. He said change is needed to bring new life, new jobs and new opportunity.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He described it as a city within a city, replacing the dead mall that had been accumulating cobwebs for the last 12 years. Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be done by 2027. The project team is still working on permitting for the rest of the development.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration in Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: 35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College. The nonprofit supports foster kids in Broward and Palm Beach County through education, adoptions and independent living resources.
cards.body:
Thirty-five foster youth and young adults graduated at ChildNet's annual celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit. Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. The organization equipped them with the resources they needed to move forward. Diaz shared a message for others in similar situations, saying, "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams. If you like push past with the pain and just keep trying hard." Saintfort echoed her message, stating, "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it and stuff."

Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, reflected on the evening's significance. "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard. We are to celebrate them," Rein said. Diaz is already enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College, where she hopes to become a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber.

cards.headline: Boynton Beach mother of 2 expecting twins faces eviction
cards.teaser: Chellizabeth Colon, 27, is a single mother of two with twins on the way who can no longer afford her rent after splitting from her husband three weeks ago. She was supposed to leave her East Boynton Beach rental home yesterday.
cards.body:
Chellizabeth Colon, 27, is a single mother of two daughters, ages 4 and 5, who is expecting twins due in August. Three weeks ago, she split from her husband, who had been paying the bills. Since then, she has fallen into financial crisis and can no longer afford rent on her East Boynton Beach home. Her landlord has told her she was supposed to leave yesterday. Colon's doctor has placed her on strict bed rest due to placenta previa, a serious pregnancy complication, but she has been packing up her house alone. "I can't really do anything. I wasn't supposed to pack up this whole house by myself, or my water could literally break," she explained. She has reached out to shelters for help, but they do not have any availability.

After hearing her story, WPTV connected Colon with The Lord's Place, a local nonprofit that has been seeing a huge need for housing in Palm Beach County. Staff from their housing services said they will be calling Colon directly. Palm Beach County's Community Services Department said their homeless services programs are reserved for individuals currently experiencing homelessness, but Colon may qualify for homeless prevention assistance depending on her circumstances and whether space is available. The county said their team will reach out to her directly to assess her situation and discuss available resources.

hero.headline: Beetlejuice Musical Runs Through June 7 at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit runs through Saturday at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, bringing spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
Beetlejuice the musical is playing at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach through June 7. Running June 2 through June 7, the Broadway hit brings its spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments to the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen, whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. I get to break the fourth wall a lot, so I get to communicate directly to the audience and share some moments with them, he explained. Very early in the run, he experienced one of those unexpected moments. I have a wig change on stage that Im wearing two wigs. The second wig came off with the first wig, so I was bald for an entire scene, and I got to play with that a little bit, and got to experience everyone seeing me for the first time and not knowing that I am bald.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50, and the safest and most secure way to get them is to buy directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens Sixth Graders Teach Computer Building, AI at Summer Camp
cards.teaser: The Weiss School hosts Kids Teaching Kids Academy, where 12-year-old founder Heath Neer and peer instructors teach students to build computers and learn artificial intelligence basics.
cards.body:
At The Weiss School this week, sixth graders are teaching their peers how to build computers and grasp the basics of artificial intelligence. The Kids Teaching Kids Academy, created by 12-year-old founder Heath Neer, launched last year with five students and has quadrupled in size this summer with 20 participants and five student instructors from Palm Beach Gardens, West Palm Beach and Riviera Beach. The free program runs June 1-4 and is entirely peer-led, supported by The Weiss School and parent volunteers.

The camp's curriculum includes hands-on assembly of computers that attendees take home free, plus lessons on fundamental AI concepts. As technology becomes increasingly vital for education and careers, programs like Kids Teaching Kids aim to close gaps in access for students who might not otherwise have a computer. The program uses donated parts and community support to keep costs down, while instructors wear camp shirts and hats that create team spirit. With day one underway, instructors plan to finish each build and move into AI application demonstrations by week's end. Organizers hope the success will encourage similar peer-led models across Palm Beach County.

cards.headline: Armory Art Center Summer Camps Run Through August in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: The Armory Art Center is debuting a lineup of camps and programs designed for artists of all ages, from splatter painting to workshops exploring global styles and cultures.
cards.body:
The Armory Art Center is kicking off summer with a lineup of camps and programs designed for artists of all ages, according to Education Director Vita Litvak. From splatter painting inspired by mid-20th-century art movements to workshops exploring global styles and cultures, the creative offerings aim to engage participants from young children to adults. The Armory's broad range of offerings, from youth camps to adult intensives, reflects a growing trend of accessible, community-based creativity.

Summer camp sessions run in various formats through August, with registration available at armoryart.org. The center offers scholarships, Litvak confirmed, ensuring that cost isn't a barrier for budding artists. As summer begins, arts organizations across Palm Beach County are working to reach residents seeking enrichment close to home.

cards.headline: 100 Paddlers to Cross 80 Miles of Ocean to Lake Worth Beach for Cystic Fibrosis
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the Atlantic Ocean in June to raise funds for families living with cystic fibrosis through the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. Event founder Travis Suit will launch participants from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, with arrivals expected at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. All proceeds benefit the Piper's Angels Foundation, which Suit established to honor his daughter, Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4. The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10, featuring a poolside social at Bimini Cove, a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner on Thursday, and a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony on Friday to honor cystic fibrosis warriors.

Safety requirements are strict. All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear during nighttime paddling. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and kept active throughout the crossing, and mandatory safety meetings will be held before launch. Paddlers must raise a minimum of $2,000, while crew members and virtual participants have a $500 minimum, with contributions due by July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong celebration to greet arriving paddlers. For more information, visit crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

hero.headline: Florida Senate Sends Homestead Property Tax Cut to November Ballot
hero.body:
Floridians will vote in November on whether to dramatically reduce homestead property taxes after the Senate voted 30-9 to place HJR 1-F on the ballot. The House passed the measure 75-26. The constitutional amendment is a major priority of Governor Ron DeSantis.

If approved by at least 60% of voters, the amendment would increase homestead exemptions for primary residences to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for those who own homes in the state by the end of this year. Further increases would be tied to the Consumer Price Index. School taxes would not be subject to the increased exemption limit and would remain at $25,000.

The measure could put money in homeowners' pockets across the state. County and city officials have warned the effort could wreak havoc on local budgets as reduced property tax revenue affects municipal services and infrastructure funding.

Floridians who own primary residences as of the end of 2026 would be eligible for the expanded exemption beginning in 2027. The vote will take place on the November ballot, requiring support from at least 60% of voters to amend the state constitution. The measure represents one of the most significant property tax reduction proposals to reach Florida voters in recent years.

cards.headline: President Trump Nominates Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez as Ambassador to Brazil
cards.teaser: House Speaker Daniel Perez, who spent two years leading the Florida House and publicly battling Governor DeSantis, has been nominated by President Donald Trump to serve as U.S. Ambassador to Brazil.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump has nominated Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez as U.S. Ambassador to Brazil, the largest country in South America and one of the United States' most significant trade and diplomatic partners in the region. The nomination was part of a broader batch of appointments Trump sent to the Senate, which also included four other Florida nominees for ambassador and federal law enforcement posts.

Perez spent the past two years leading the Florida House, publicly battling DeSantis while moving the Legislature toward a more coequal footing. The nomination comes just under nine months after the White House urged Perez to run for Florida Attorney General, an undertaking he declined to pursue that would have put him on a collision course with DeSantis appointee James Uthmeier.

cards.headline: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings Suspends Governor Campaign After Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
cards.teaser: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings is suspending his campaign for Governor after receiving a prostate cancer diagnosis this week.
cards.body:
Jerry Demings suspended his campaign for Governor after he was diagnosed with prostate cancer. Demings said he received the diagnosis on Monday, then told his children on Thursday that he was quitting the campaign. Demings said he plans on running through the finish line as Orange County Mayor and serving the remaining six months of his term.

Demings said he was optimistic about his prognosis. He reminded the public that 1 in 6 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer. The odds worsen for African American men, where it is 1 in 4, Demings added.

Demings explained his decision to leave the race. In order for me to receive the treatment that I need, I am going to have to come off the campaign trail, Demings said. I have to let something go. I can't continue to do my job as Mayor, take care of my family and run for Governor. So, I made a difficult decision.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds Calls for GOP Unity, Refuses Debates as Opponents Demand Debate Stage
cards.teaser: Republican Byron Donalds, who has raised $81.1 million for his gubernatorial run, says the party should coalesce behind him and refuses to participate in primary debates.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds says he is the front-runner in the race for the Republican gubernatorial nomination and that the party should coalesce behind him more than two months before the August 18 Primary. The Naples Republican made this call for party unity Friday, hours after Jerry Demings announced he was ending his campaign because of a prostate cancer diagnosis. Donalds, who has raised $81 million so far, said the general election starts today and that he would rather deploy those resources in the General Election than in the Primary given that Democrats have a presumptive nominee in the wake of Demings' departure. He cites his endorsement from President Donald Trump and notes that he is up by more than 40 points in multiple public polls as proof of his viability. All other candidates are in single digits, Donalds said.

Jay Collins and former House Speaker Paul Renner both insist that debates are necessary. Collins launched The Collins Callout website Friday, which concedes that Donalds is the prohibitive front-runner. Renner posted a video to social media Friday saying neither Collins nor Donalds is willing to debate him, imploring them to get on stage so Floridians can see the differences between candidates. Fundraising reports for Collins and Renner covering activity through May are due June 10. Through the last report covering activity through the end of March, Renner had raised more than $6 million and Collins roughly $1.75 million.

cards.headline: Florida State University Graduates First Veterans Entrepreneurship Cohort in Leon County
cards.teaser: Fourteen veterans completed a six-week business training program at Florida State University designed to help them turn business ideas into viable ventures.
cards.body:
Florida State University's Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship graduated the first Leon County cohort of its Veteran Entrepreneurship Certificate Program this week, a partnership with Veterans Florida. Fourteen veterans completed the six-week Facilitated Business Modeling Program, which focuses on customer discovery, market validation and entrepreneurial decision-making. Participants ranged from aspiring entrepreneurs with early-stage concepts to business owners looking to refine and grow existing operations. The program combines workshops, mentoring and applied exercises designed to help participants evaluate opportunities and strengthen business concepts. Veterans also connected with local entrepreneurial resources and learned from FSU faculty members, including Susana Santos, Bill Lickson, Juliana Binhote, Doug Tatum and Melissa Robert.

Eric Liguori, associate dean for Research and External Relations at the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship who led the program, said veterans bring an incredible combination of resilience, leadership and adaptability to entrepreneurship. Graduates received certificates of completion and are now eligible to join the Jim Moran Institute for Global Entrepreneurship's statewide alum network of more than 2,700 Florida business owners. Susan Fiorito, dean of the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship, noted the partnership reflects community-centered impact and expressed pride in supporting veterans and military-connected families as they pursue entrepreneurial opportunities.

cards.headline: Democrat Benjamin Sandlin Launches Second Run for Jacksonville House District 12
cards.teaser: Benjamin Sandlin filed Friday for Jacksonville's HD 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago.
cards.body:
Democrat Benjamin Sandlin is launching a second run in Jacksonville's HD 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago. The Republican-leaning seat is open because Duggan is term-limited. The 22-year-old repeat candidate filed for the House race Friday, just three days before the beginning of qualifying on Monday, June 8. Sandlin said the Florida Democratic Party and he had been talking and that they agreed that this seat was just too close in 24 to leave uncontested. He told Florida Politics on Saturday morning that it would be a huge missed opportunity to have an extra voice for labor rights, public schools and housing justice in the Legislature. As the sole Democrat in HD 12, it is likely Sandlin will advance to the November ballot upon qualifying.

Former Jacksonville City Council President Terrance Freeman is running in HD 12 to succeed Duggan. Freeman is well-positioned for his Primary. Through the end of May, he raised more than $167,000 to his campaign account and an additional $506,000 to an affiliated political committee, For the Future We Want. He had roughly $390,000 on hand at the end of last month. Freeman was appointed to the Jacksonville City Council in 2018 by former Gov. Rick Scott to fill a vacancy. He was then elected to at-large, countywide seats in 2019 and 2023, and served a year as Council President.

cards.headline: Gatorland Opens New Craft Beer Bar with Exclusive Crooked Can Brewery Lager
cards.teaser: Gatorland opened the Guzzlin Gator Beverage Barn on Memorial Day Weekend and is now selling an exclusive craft beer made by Crooked Can Brewery.
cards.body:
Gatorland opened the Guzzlin' Gator Beverage Barn on Memorial Day Weekend, an outdoor, shaded bar located near the Legends of the Swamp show. The bar serves the Grinnin' Gator lager, an exclusive craft beer made by Crooked Can Brewery that can only be found at the park, along with five other pours including Orlando's Ivanhoe Park and Orange Blossom breweries and St. Petersburg's 3 Daughters Brewing. Crooked Can Brewery, based in Winter Gardens, settled on a Pale German lager with hints of citrus for the collaboration. "Ultimately we wanted to provide a beer that was kind of a beer for everybody, which is why we landed on that pale lager," said Alan Delahunt, Managing Partner at Crooked Can Brewing Company.

Tim Acheson, Gatorland's Director of Food and Beverage, described the beer as a "summertime sipper" with citrus notes including grapefruit and orange peel. Acheson is envisioning expansion of the menu with kiddie cocktails and dirty sodas to accommodate families with kids. The Grinnin' Gator is currently served in plastic cups, but Gatorland plans to sell six-packs with decorative cans in the gift shop for guests to take home. Acheson also teased that other beer collaborations are in development at Gatorland.

hero.headline: Ocean could breach Jupiter Island at Peck Lake, potentially splitting island in half
hero.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island faces severe coastal erosion across its entire 11.5-mile shoreline. The most concerning threat is at Peck Lake, where a breach could split the island in half by turning a thin strip of land into an open inlet. This risk extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand, demonstrating that such events are not merely theoretical concerns.

The erosion threatens far more than just the physical coastline. Roads, buildings, and drainage systems face damage, but the report also documents risks to natural habitats, wildlife, and archaeological sites. Among the most significant is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old site that has already lost half its area to erosion. Other endangered locations include Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society noted that more than 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. Perry explained that future breaches could destabilize ecosystems dependent on a careful balance between fresh and saltwater environments. He emphasized the urgency of the situation, stating "the last 15 years, it's been rising at a faster rate" regarding sea level rise since the 1950s.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town actively combats erosion through ongoing maintenance efforts. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project that deposited enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field stressed that oceanfront homes remain safe only because of these continuous interventions. He described the approach as "just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," acknowledging it is a temporary solution. The town invests approximately $3 million in annual taxpayer funding toward beach renourishment.

However, this funding strategy depends on continued financial support. If a breach occurs, Field warned that repairs would require substantial state and federal investment. He cautioned that "if funding ever goes away for beach renourishment in Florida, the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly, and not in a way that anybody's particularly happy with." Field noted that the recent FDEP assessment should help Jupiter Island compete more effectively for state and federal funding to address erosion. The report positions the island to make a stronger case for future financial support to mitigate these mounting coastal threats.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties
cards.teaser: A seasonal ban on fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen takes effect June 1 in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties to reduce nutrient runoff during rainy season.
cards.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have implemented a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen beginning June 1. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, said the ban is designed to help reduce nutrient rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms that disrupt waterways like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River.

According to Skaggs, these blooms can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a good alternative during the ban for gardens and landscaping. Ricketts said a small trash can is the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to your landscape.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue extinguishes nearly 40-acre brush fire in Indiantown
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue put out a brush fire covering nearly 40 acres in Indiantown.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a nearly 40-acre brush fire in Indiantown. The fire was brought under control by county firefighters.

The incident occurred in the Indiantown area of Martin County. Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the blaze and contained it.

cards.headline: Law enforcement pursuit slows northbound I-95 traffic near Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: A brief law enforcement pursuit caused traffic delays on northbound Interstate 95 near Hobe Sound.
cards.body:
A brief law enforcement pursuit slowed northbound Interstate 95 traffic near Hobe Sound. The pursuit affected traffic flow on the highway.

The incident took place on northbound I-95 in the Hobe Sound area. Law enforcement was involved in the pursuit that caused the traffic slowdown.

cards.headline: Martin County updates emergency dispatch center
cards.teaser: Martin County has revamped its emergency dispatch center with new upgrades.
cards.body:
Martin County has completed upgrades to its emergency dispatch center. The revamped center will handle emergency calls for the county.

The dispatch center serves Martin County residents and coordinates emergency response. The county completed the updates to improve emergency services.

cards.headline: Stuart resident Brian Warren dies
cards.teaser: Brian Warren of Stuart passed away in 2026.
cards.body:
Brian Warren, a resident of Stuart, died in 2026. Services are being handled by All County Funeral Home & Crematory Treasure Coast Chapel.

Warren lived in Stuart in Martin County. The family has made arrangements through the local funeral home.

cards.headline: Dr. Stuart Bell being considered for University of Florida president
cards.teaser: Dr. Stuart R. Bell is the sole finalist for president of the University of Florida and has discussed his intentions regarding athletics.
cards.body:
Dr. Stuart Bell is the sole finalist for the position of president at the University of Florida. Bell has gone in-depth on his intention to be involved in athletics at the university.

Bell discussed his plans for involvement with UF athletics programs. Supporters have written columns explaining why Bell is the right choice for the University of Florida presidency.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect June 30 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will be prohibited from using fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The restriction is designed to run through the rainy season and aims to prevent nutrient-rich runoff from entering local waterways, where it can trigger harmful algae blooms.

Jordan Skaggs, a representative with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that the ban directly targets fertilizers that contribute to destructive algae blooms in sensitive ecosystems like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. These blooms can have serious consequences for the environment. They block out beneficial aquatic plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. In some cases, when algae blooms reach high densities, they produce toxins that pose risks to human health, harm wildlife populations and damage the overall health of aquatic ecosystems.

For residents concerned about maintaining their gardens and landscaping during the ban, Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical alternative. Ricketts noted that composting can be as simple as using a small container and represents an effective, practical method for adding nutrients back into your landscape without relying on chemical fertilizers.

The seasonal fertilizer ban applies uniformly across all three Treasure Coast counties, making compliance important for all residents in the affected areas. Those who use fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen after June 30 may face penalties. The regulation reflects growing efforts in Florida to protect waterways from nutrient pollution and the harmful algal blooms that can result from excessive nutrient runoff during heavy rain periods.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after homeowner watches burglary on security camera
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man was arrested after a homeowner spotted a burglary in progress on a security camera.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested after a homeowner spotted a burglary in progress on a security camera. The homeowner was able to alert police to the break-in as it happened.

Police responded to the scene and arrested the suspect. The security camera footage provided evidence of the burglary in progress.

The arrest highlights how home security systems can help homeowners and law enforcement respond quickly to crimes. The suspect now faces burglary charges.

cards.headline: Lowe's opens new 94,000-square-foot store in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A new Lowe's home improvement store opened in Port St. Lucie, bringing 94,000 square feet of retail space to the area.
cards.body:
A new Lowe's home improvement store opened in Port St. Lucie, bringing 94,000 square feet of retail space to the area. The store is now serving customers in the growing Port St. Lucie market.

The 94,000-square-foot facility adds to the retail options available to Port St. Lucie residents. The store offers home improvement supplies, tools, and materials.

The opening reflects continued commercial development in Port St. Lucie. The new location joins other Lowe's stores serving the Treasure Coast region.

cards.headline: Florida Highway Patrol recovers stolen vehicle, arrests driver in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Florida Highway Patrol recovered a stolen vehicle and arrested the driver in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 30 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents of Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop applying fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen to their lawns and landscaping. The seasonal restriction targets the rainy season, when nutrient-rich runoff can wash into local waterways and trigger algae blooms that damage aquatic ecosystems.

According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the ban aims to reduce the nutrient pollution that feeds these harmful blooms. The blooms pose a serious threat to waterways including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," Skaggs explained. Beyond blocking sunlight, these blooms can become dangerous at high concentrations. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health."

Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical alternative during the ban period. Instead of applying chemical fertilizers to gardens and landscaping, residents can build their own compost systems. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." This method allows homeowners to continue enriching their soil without relying on phosphorus and nitrogen products.

The fertilizer restriction applies to all residential lawn and landscaping applications during the rainy season in the three-county area. Residents should prepare now to transition away from traditional fertilizers before the June 30 deadline takes effect. For those seeking guidance on composting techniques or other sustainable landscaping practices, local extension offices can provide additional resources and support.
